original_value: This paper presents a general-purpose formulation of a large class of discrete-time planning problems, with hybrid state and control-spaces, as factored transition systems. Factoring allows state transitions to be described as the intersection of several constraints each affecting a subset of the state and control variables. Robotic manipulation problems with many movable objects involve constraints that only affect several variables at a time and therefore exhibit large amounts of factoring. We develop a theoretical framework for solving factored transition systems with sampling-based algorithms. The framework characterizes conditions on the submanifold in which solutions lie, leading to a characterization of robust feasibility that incorporates dimensionality-reducing constraints. It then connects those conditions to corresponding conditional samplers that can be composed to produce values on this submanifold. We present two domain-independent, probabilistically complete planning algorithms that take, as input, a set of conditional samplers. We demonstrate the empirical efficiency of these algorithms on a set of challenging task and motion planning problems involving picking, placing, and pushing.

result.paraphrase: This paper develops a general formulation for a broad class of discrete-time planning problems with hybrid state and control spaces by modeling them as factored transition systems. Such factoring expresses state transitions as the intersection of multiple constraints, each acting on only a subset of state and control variables. Robotic manipulation tasks with many movable objects typically contain constraints that involve only a few variables at a time, and thus show substantial factoring. We propose a theoretical framework for solving factored transition systems using sampling-based algorithms. The framework identifies conditions on the submanifold where solutions reside, yielding a notion of robust feasibility that accounts for dimensionality-reducing constraints. It then links those conditions to conditional samplers that can be composed to generate values on this submanifold. We introduce two domain-independent, probabilistically complete planning algorithms that accept a set of conditional samplers as input. We demonstrate their empirical efficiency on challenging task-and-motion planning problems involving picking, placing, and pushing.
